body.text: Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive should be seen as a national security threat. The issues are Chinese intelligence penetration, corporate governance of a strategically important company and the integrity of Washington’s decision-making.

The scandal goes to the heart of whether commercial interests have undermined national security policies designed to preserve the United States’ technological and military advantage over China – which is vital for all US allies, including Australia.

Huang has not only engaged in a romantic relationship with a Chinese business associate who was at least subject to potential control by China’s state security apparatus and may well have been its active and diligent agent. With this appalling decision alone, he has risked US and wider democratic security.

But he has also used his influence to secure looser US restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors to China. His arguments, including that China will develop its own artificial intelligence capabilities regardless of American restrictions, would be funny if the circumstances weren’t so serious. The fact that a strategic competitor might eventually develop a capability is no justification for helping it get there sooner. America didn’t hand over its most advanced technology to the USSR on the basis that the Soviets would eventually, one day, be able to develop it independently.

Part of the problem is public confusion from governments’ inconsistent messaging about the complex relationship with China. Almost every democracy is beholden to trade with China, so political speeches go out of their way to express the importance of China as an economic partner and to avoid any reference to it as a strategic rival. The closest many democratic leaders get these days is to refer to ‘differences’, while US President Donald Trump facilitates a false equivalence by saying that the US also spies.

Huang’s reinstatement, including the personal intervention by Trump that promoted it, amplifies the national security threat posed by the relationship between commercial influence and national decision making. The central issue is whether the company’s commercial interests have been allowed to influence decisions that should be determined by America’s national security priorities.

There are signs the US has recognised the seriousness of the threat. Following revelations that Nvidia’s advanced chips were getting to China, congressional scrutiny (including investigations supported by Republicans) kicked into gear. Tighter enforcement of security laws should make it considerably harder for advanced chips to reach China through intermediaries. These investigations will need to establish how export controls failed, who facilitated the diversion of advanced chips, whether Chinese intelligence was involved and whether commercial interests compromised American national security.

Does Huang’s reinstatement mean we’re returning to non-enforcement of the export restrictions? The congressional investigations and public scrutiny likely mean the answer is no. Those working for China will have greater difficulty in getting advanced chips to it.
So China will remain concerned about restrictions that limit its access to the computing power it needs to compete with the US.

Unlike such stolen state secrets as weapon performance, high-performance chips for AI data centres don’t last long: they wear out within years. But China still wants them. It wants whatever it can get to advance its technological ambitions. Advanced chips can particularly help it accelerate in three key areas of direct threat to the US and its allies.

First, they can push forward China’s military modernisation. Advanced computing is increasingly central to the development of autonomous weapons, including aerial and naval drones, and other systems that will shape future warfare. This undermines the multi-billion-dollar efforts of AUKUS partners Australia, Britain and the US to answer the military challenge posed by China. Yet an American company, Nvidia, has pursued commercial opportunities that helped provide China with computing capabilities to strengthen the very military forces AUKUS is intended to deter.
This means we are investing in military capabilities to defend against military capabilities being developed with American tech. That’s the opposite of a national security strategy.

Second, greater computing power strengthens China’s cyber and intelligence capabilities. It can help identify vulnerabilities in Western networks, improve espionage capabilities and facilitate the theft of sensitive information and intellectual property.

Third, advanced chips enable Chinese companies and research institutions to train increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models. The competition to develop frontier AI is fundamentally a competition between the US and China and yet here is an American company helping China in that race.

The cumulative effect is to undermine America’s technological and military advantage. Why would Washington voluntarily accelerate the technological development of the country it identifies as its principal strategic competitor? Beijing has made no secret of its ambitions. Its Made in China 2025 strategy, announced in 2015, explicitly sought to displace the US as the world’s leading technological and military power by establishing Chinese dominance across strategically important industries – though this only made clear what every five-year plan from Beijing had aimed at for decades.
Advanced Nvidia chips directly support those ambitions, a problem not just for the US but for all of America’s Asia-Pacific allies, including Australia, Japan and the Philippines, and for Taiwan.
Australia can learn lessons from this.

Foreign interference and influence are not confined to governments. The leadership, commercial relationships and governance of strategically important technology companies must also be considered national security matters. Understanding of this is lacking even in some defence companies, and it is almost non-existent for businesses that feed advanced dual-use technology to them.

Australia should review whether any tech companies are helping China’s technological and military-industrial ecosystem, whether by supplying dual-use technologies directly or cooperating with it in scientific and engineering research. At the very least, any company or university that chooses to supply China should be prohibited from participating in any aspect of AUKUS. If the company or university has technology that the security partnership can’t easily get elsewhere, it should instead be prohibited from dealing with China.

Importantly, Australia and other American allies should not allow the Nvidia scandal to be passed off as an internal American affair. The principle applies everywhere: national security must not be subordinated to commercial revenue. The US needs to demonstrate that it understands that principle. Australia should insist on it, too.
